match.reason: No point in the bank covers budgets: related points such as monitoring performance and business plans touch on planning and control, but none teaches operating, project and financial budgets.

draft.title: Budgets
card: A budget is a plan of expected income and spending for a future period. A business sets it before the period starts.
plans the income and expenses of day-to-day activity, such as sales, wages and materials.
plans the expected costs and income of one job with a start and an end, such as building a new store.
plans the business's cash and funding, such as expected cash flow and borrowing. Managers compare actual results with each budget, and a gap shows where to investigate and act.
draft.remember: A budget is a plan set in advance, and comparing it with actual results helps managers control the business.

a.q: At the end of the month, Tanya compares her café's actual wage costs with the budgeted amount and finds they are higher. How does the budget help her?
opts: It shows a gap to investigate and act on
It lowers the wage costs by itself
It records what the café owns and owes
It shows the profit the café has already earned
a.why: A budget gives a planned figure to compare with actual results. The gap shows where to look and act. A budget does not change costs by itself, because managers must take action.
a.clue: Think about what the planned figure is compared with.

b.q: Dev's building firm in Ballarat is about to start a single new apartment block, and he wants to plan the expected costs and income of that job alone. Which budget suits this?
opts: A budget for last year's results
b.why: A project budget covers one job with a start and an end, such as one apartment block. An operating budget is the tempting wrong answer because it covers ongoing day-to-day activity, not a single job.
b.clue: The job has a start and an end.

a.best: It shows a gap to investigate and act on
